subject: Maths
central_question: How can ruler-and-compass constructions and tiling arguments create exact geometric designs and determine whether shapes cover a region without gaps or overlaps?
in_scope_units: 6.1 Geometric Constructions—Eyes: using equal-radius arcs to locate points on a perpendicular bisector and construct a symmetric eye.
Perpendicular Bisector and Bisection: proving through congruent triangles that the constructed line passes through the midpoint at 90°.
Construction of a 90° Angle at a Given Point and Śulba-Sūtras: adapting the perpendicular-bisector method and using a folded-rope construction.
Angle Bisection for a Design: constructing equal halves of any angle and obtaining 45° from 90°.
Repeating Units and Repeating Angles: copying an angle exactly with a ruler and compass.
Construction of Parallel Lines and Arch Designs: transferring equal angles to create parallel lines, trefoil arches and pointed arches.
Regular Hexagons and Equilateral Triangles: using six 60° angles around a point to construct a regular hexagon.
Related Constructions: constructing 30°, 15°, a six-pointed star, inflexed arcs and perpendiculars through an external point.
6.2 Tiling—Tangrams and Rectangular Grids: covering regions without gaps or overlaps and testing 2 × 1 domino tilings.
Checkerboard Reasoning and Plane Tilings: using parity and colour balance, then exploring squares, equilateral triangles, regular hexagons, Escher tilings and honeycomb cells.
Chapter Figure it Out activities: applying construction and tiling reasoning throughout the chapter.
banned_topics: Construction of a regular pentagon, which the chapter explicitly postpones to later years.
Area formulas for circles and polygons.
Advanced symmetry groups and formal topology.

known_pitfalls.claim: Any two arcs drawn from the endpoints of a segment will produce its perpendicular bisector.
known_pitfalls.correction: For each intersection point, the arcs from the two endpoints must use the same radius and must be long enough to meet.

known_pitfalls.claim: A perpendicular bisector only makes a right angle.
known_pitfalls.correction: It must both be perpendicular to the segment and pass through its midpoint.

known_pitfalls.claim: To bisect an angle, the arcs drawn from the two marked points may use different radii.
known_pitfalls.correction: Those two arcs must use the same radius so their intersection is equally distant from both marked points.

known_pitfalls.claim: A region with an even number of unit squares is always tileable by 2 × 1 tiles.
known_pitfalls.correction: Even area is necessary but not sufficient; the shape and checkerboard colour balance can still make tiling impossible.

known_pitfalls.claim: Any regular polygon can tile the plane by itself.
known_pitfalls.correction: The chapter demonstrates tilings with squares, equilateral triangles and regular hexagons, not every regular polygon.

known_pitfalls.claim: The chapter gives a complete ruler-and-compass construction of a regular pentagon.
known_pitfalls.correction: It states that regular-pentagon construction needs ideas to be studied in later years.

recommended_example_progression: Begin with the 'Eyes' construction and Fig. 6.1 to construct and justify a perpendicular bisector.
Use Figs. 6.2–6.4 to construct a 90° angle at a point and reproduce the Śulba-Sūtra rope method.
Use the Steps for Angle Bisection on pages 143–144 to obtain 45° and justify the construction by SSS.
Use the Steps of Construction to Copy an Angle on page 146 and the parallel-line construction in Figs. 6.7–6.10.
Use the arch activities and the regular-hexagon construction on pages 149–154.
Use the 4 × 6, 4 × 7 and 5 × 7 grid questions and checkerboard examples on pages 157–159.
Conclude with plane tilings by regular polygons, Escher designs and hexagonal cells on pages 160–163.
ncert_end_of_chapter_exercises_reference: The chapter contains several section-wise Figure it Out construction and tiling activities rather than one consolidated numbered end exercise, followed by the summary on page 163.
